```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(malariafwd)
```

A run takes `r length(vivax_params())` parameters, and `vivax_params()` gives every one a
default, so a first run needs none of them. `?vivax_params` lists them all with their units and
bounds, and `param_info()` returns the same thing as a table. This page is about the smaller set
you have to think about: the ones where a plausible-looking value quietly changes what you are
measuring.

Four things catch people out, and two more are worth knowing before you start. All six come
before the per-parameter table.

## The defaults are a transparent model, not a realistic one

Five parameters ship at the value that switches their mechanism **off**, so a first run shows the
model's mechanics with no carriage or observation layer on top of them:

```{r}
off <- param_info(c("P_PRIMARY", "P_GAMETOCYTE", "GAMETOCYTE_DELAY",
                    "P_DETECT_PRIMARY", "P_DETECT_RELAPSE"))
knitr::kable(off[, c("name", "default", "meaning")],
             col.names = c("Parameter", "Default", "What it does"))
```

At those defaults every transmitted genotype becomes a blood-stage infection, is infectious to
mosquitoes from the next day, and is detected. That is deliberate: it means a discrepancy in
your output is the model's, not that of a layer you did not know was on. It is also not
*P. vivax*. Gametocytes
appear early but not instantly, carriage is high but incomplete, and relapses are often
sub-patent — so a result you intend to publish should move these off their defaults and report
the sensitivity. The per-parameter table below gives the ranges to sweep.

## Transmission is scale-dependent, and `BITING_RATE` is not a biting rate

`BITING_RATE` is the daily probability that *one mosquito* bites. The bites a human receives per
day are

```{r}
p <- vivax_params()
unname(p$BITING_RATE * p$N_MOSQ / p$N_HOSTS)
```

so the same `BITING_RATE` means different exposure at a different `N_MOSQ` / `N_HOSTS` ratio.

The *transmission rate* depends only on that product, so `BITING_RATE` and `N_MOSQ` trade off
against each other — but the genetics do not. Halving `BITING_RATE` and doubling `N_MOSQ` leaves
exposure unchanged while spreading the same uptakes over twice as many mosquitoes, each of which
then carries fewer lineages and so co-transmits and outcrosses less. For a transmission-rate
sweep, vary one of the two; where a result turns on co-transmission or on recombination in the
midgut, hold `N_MOSQ` fixed and vary `BITING_RATE`.

Prevalence and complexity of infection are scale-dependent in their own right — a small
population loses diversity to drift faster, and saturates differently — so **a transmission rate
fitted on 40 hosts does not transfer to 4,000**. Calibrate at the population size you intend to
publish, not at the size that was quick to fit.

## The uptake lambdas are rates before truncation, not mean counts

`LAMBDA_OOCYSTS` and `LAMBDA_SPOROZOITES` parameterise *zero-truncated* draws: the model has
already decided that transmission happened, so the count it needs is conditioned away from zero.
Conditioning pulls the realised mean up, and the gap is largest exactly where feeding studies
report their numbers. A lambda of 2 does not give a mean of 2:

```{r}
uptake_moments(2)          # Poisson
uptake_moments(2, k = 1)   # negative binomial, same lambda, more spread
```

So a mean oocyst count read off a paper cannot be set as a lambda. Convert it first. Membrane
feeds of wild *An. arabiensis* in Ethiopia give a median of 7.2 oocysts per midgut (Ayele et al.
2023), well above the default's realised 2.31 — to simulate that, ask for it as a target:

```{r}
uptake_calibrate(7.2)              # a target realised mean
uptake_calibrate(7.2, var = 60)    # and a target variance, if you have one
```

`uptake_calibrate()` returns the `lambda` and `k` to set, with the moments they achieve.

## Two parameters are guards, not quantities

`MAX_MOI` and `MAX_LINEAGES_PER_MOSQ` exist to stop a run growing without bound. They are not
biology, and at their defaults of 20 they should never bind. Set one low and it stops being a
guard and becomes the thing your run measures — a `MAX_MOI` of 3 does not model an immune
ceiling at 3, it truncates superinfection and silently stops topping up the hypnozoite
reservoir of the hosts it refuses.

Check that they did not bind. A mosquito's `moi_active` is exactly the count the cap tests:

```{r}
mosq <- load_state(example_run(), entity = "mosquito")
max(mosq$moi_active)                                   # against MAX_LINEAGES_PER_MOSQ
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
carried <- mosq[moi_active > 0]
peak    <- max(carried$moi_active)
allowed <- vivax_params()$MAX_LINEAGES_PER_MOSQ
n_at_peak <- length(unique(carried[moi_active == peak]$entity_id))
n_ever    <- length(unique(carried$entity_id))
days_peak <- nrow(carried[moi_active == peak])
```

In this small bundled run just `r n_at_peak` of the `r n_ever` mosquitoes ever infected reached
`r peak` of the `r allowed` lineages it was allowed, on `r days_peak` of
`r format(nrow(carried), big.mark = ",")` infected mosquito-days. The guard held, but with only
`r allowed - peak` lineages to spare — which is why it is worth looking rather than assuming.

For a host, `MAX_MOI` counts the blood-stage lineages it carries whether or not they are patent,
so sum the two columns (this omits clones gained earlier the same day, making it a close lower
bound):

```{r}
host <- load_state(example_run())
max(host$moi_active + host$moi_subpatent)              # against MAX_MOI
```

## Changing diversity without changing the epidemic

Founding diversity and establishment are separable, and conflating them is the commonest way to
confound a relatedness result. `N_FOUNDER_HOSTS` sets how many hosts start infected, and so
whether the epidemic takes off at all; `N_FOUNDER_LINEAGES` sets how many *distinct* genomes
those hosts carry, the rest being clonal copies. Hold the first fixed and lower the second to
raise background relatedness while leaving establishment alone:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
diverse <- vivax_params(N_FOUNDER_HOSTS = 12, N_FOUNDER_LINEAGES = 12)  # maximal diversity
related <- vivax_params(N_FOUNDER_HOSTS = 12, N_FOUNDER_LINEAGES = 3)   # same epidemic, more IBD
```

## Tropical or temperate, reported separately

`ALPHA_ACTIVATE` and `K_LATENCY` together set relapse periodicity, and so how distinguishable a
relapse is from a reinfection — the quantity much of this package exists to measure. At
`K_LATENCY = 0` the reservoir is tropical: a hypnozoite can activate immediately. `K_LATENCY = 2`
with `DELTA_LATENCY` gives the temperate pattern, with a delay first.

These are different epidemiologies, not a range to average over. Report them as separate
scenarios.

## How to choose each of them

The table below is generated from the package's parameter dictionary, so it cannot drift from
`?vivax_params`. It covers the parameters that carry explicit guidance; the rest are documented
in `?vivax_params` and in section 10 of the
[model description](https://shaziaruybal.github.io/malariafwd/MODEL_DESCRIPTION.html). The `S`
numbers point to the sensitivity-analysis table in the
[roadmap](https://shaziaruybal.github.io/malariafwd/ROADMAP.html), which gives the evidence
behind each recommendation.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
info <- as.data.frame(param_info())
info <- info[!is.na(info$setting), ]
capitalise <- function(x) sub("^(.)", "\\U\\1", x, perl = TRUE)
for (g in unique(info$group)) {
  rows <- info[info$group == g, ]
  cat("\n###", g, "\n\n")
  tbl <- data.frame(
    Parameter = paste0("`", rows$name, "`"),
    Default = paste0("`", rows$default, "`"),
    `How to choose one` = paste0(capitalise(rows$setting), "."),
    check.names = FALSE)
  cat(knitr::kable(tbl, row.names = FALSE), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n")
}
```

## Sweeping rather than guessing

Where the table says *sweep*, `run_grid()` takes the parameter sets and the seeds and runs them
in parallel:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
grid <- run_grid(
  params = lapply(c(0.15, 0.4, 0.7, 1.0),
                  function(d) vivax_params(P_DETECT_RELAPSE = d, SIM_DAYS = 730)),
  seeds  = 1:20,
  outdir = file.path(tempdir(), "detect-sweep"))
```

Two habits make a sweep interpretable. Vary one mechanism at a time, since several of these
parameters move prevalence, COI and relatedness together and a joint change cannot be attributed
afterwards. And use enough seeds: at a small `N_HOSTS` the seed-to-seed spread can exceed the
effect you are testing, so a difference between two single runs is not a result.

## Where the defaults came from

`param_info()$source` gives the origin of each default in one line, and `?vivax_params` shows it
alongside the parameter. Section 13 of the
[model description](https://shaziaruybal.github.io/malariafwd/MODEL_DESCRIPTION.html) records what
has been calibrated and against which targets, and what remains a literature assumption —
`NU_HYPNOZOITE_BATCH` was fitted for one setting and should be re-fitted for yours, and
`MEAN_RECRUD_DELAY` has no estimate from data at all. The roadmap's sensitivity table lists the
eleven places where a choice most needs testing.
